# Check In … DOJ v Judge Garaufis

 September 29, 2026 

 

Checking in on the back and forth between the DOJ and Judge Nicholas Garaufis (E.D.N.Y.).
...
Yesterday, the DOJ filed a petition in the Second Circuit requesting “that the Court swiftly issue a writ of mandamus directing [Judge Garaufis] to grant the government’s motion to dismiss the remaining counts of the indictment with prejudice.”

The petition presents the following issue: “Whether the district court exceeded its authority under the Constitution and Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 48(a) by denying the government’s unopposed motion to dismiss with prejudice the indictment against five defendants.”
...
> 
> As a result, after months of efforts by the government, the district court ultimately issued an order denying the motion to dismiss the remaining charges. The district court went so far as to suggest that the government would have to provide “expert reports” to justify an unopposed motion dismissing these criminal charges. The government and the district court have profoundly different views on the nature of Rule 48 and the constitutional role of a district judge, leading to this impasse that can be resolved only by a higher court.
> 
> It appears that no appellate court has ever upheld a district court’s refusal to grant a Rule 48(a) motion. This Court should not be the first. As other circuits have ruled in similar circumstances, mandamus is necessary to remedy the district court’s dangerous and unconstitutional arrogation of executive power.”

NICHOLAS G. GARAUFIS, United States District Judge. By Memorandum and Order dated August 10, 2026 (the "Au gust 10 Order"), the court granted in part and reserved decision in part on the U.S. Department of Justice's Rule 48(a) Motion. 1 (August 10 Order (Dkt. 49); see also Rule 48(a) Mot. (Dkt. 23).) Now pending before the court is the Department's request for the court to grant the pending portions of its Motion and dismiss with prejudice Counts One and Five as alleged against the remaining defendants: Non-Appearing Defendants Ranjit Gupta, Cyril Cabanes, Saurabh Agarwal, Deepak Malhotra, and RupeshAgarwal. (McCotter Ltr. Dated 8/14/2026 ("Aug. 14 Ltr.") (Dkt. 56).) For the reasons thoroughly explained on pages 22-44 of the Au gust 10 Order-the entirety of which is fully incorporated by reference herein-and the additional reasons that follow, the government has not provided sufficient factual information to support the stated reasons to dismiss Counts One and Five. Given

the failure to satisfy this threshold, procedural requirement of 
Rule 48 (a), the court DENIES the pending portions of the Depart 
ment's Rule 48(a) Motion WITHOlIT PREJUDICE. 
I. BACKGROUND 
The court assumes familiarity with the factual background and 
procedural history of this case as set forth in its prior orders dated 
June 26, July 8, July 15, and August 10, 2026. (See August 10 Or 
der at 2-17 (summarizing the background facts and procedural 
history).) Therefore, the court provides a brief recitation of only 
the pertinent facts and procedural developments in this case be 
tween August 10, and September 3, 2026. 
A. The August 10 Order 
On August 10, the court reserved judgment on the portions of the 
Rule 48(a) Motion requesting dismissal of Counts One and Five 
against Non-Appearing Defendants with prejudice "pending the 
Department's fulfillment of its Rule 48(a) obligations as to these 
Counts." (Id. at 2.) The court directed the Department to "pro 
vide the court with sufficient factual support for each reason" for 
the requested dismissal of Counts One and Five by August 31, 
2026. (Id. at 46.) 
B. The August 11 Letter 
On August 11, R. Trent Mccotter-now, the Acting Deputy At 
torney General-submitted a letter "in response" to the 
August 10 Order. (McCotter Ltr. Dated 8/11/2026 ("Aug. 11 
Ltr.") (Dkt. SO) at 1.) Therein, Mccotter incorrectly asserted that 
the court had "disagreed" with a "number of [his] stated reasons" 
for the requested dismissal of Counts One and Five; "urge [ d]" the 
court to "reconsider its rejection of those reasons"; and set a 
deadline-stating that if the court did not "dismiss the remaining
...
the [Rule 48(a) Motion] to allow for appellate relief." (Id. at 2.) II. DISCUSSION As detailed in this court's prior orders, the court's role on a Rule 48(a) motion is narrow and distinctly judicial: "to ensure the Executive satisfies the Rule's procedural and substantive com ponents." (August 10 Order at 20; see also June 26 Order (Dkt. 36) at 3-4.) Given McCotter's apparent confusion regarding these distinct components, the court proceeds first by clarifying Rule 48 (a)'s requirements and then by explaining why-as to the requested dismissal of Counts One and Five-the procedural re quirements are not met on the current record. A. Rule 48(a)'s Requirements As detailed in the August 10 Order, Rule 48(a)'s procedural com ponent has two requirements: the government must provide "a statement of reasons and underlying factual basis." (August 10 Order at 20 (emphasis added).) Specifically, the government must provide both: (1) its actual reasons for the requested dis missal (the "proffered rationale"); and (2) "sufficient factual information" for the court to ''be satisfied" that the proffered ra tionale is both "real" and "substantial." (Id. at 21.) For the factual basis to be "sufficient," the government must provide more than bare conclusions and unsupported statements. (See id. at 20 (col lecting cases)). Instead, the government must give the court the specific facts-the evidence-allowing the court to reach the proffered rationale from the evidence presented. See United States v. Adams, 777 F. Supp. 3d 185,227 (S.D.N.Y. 2025) (citing Dep'tof Com. v. New York, 588 U.S. 752, 785 (2019)). Put differ ently,
...
B. Analysis In light of McCotter's refusal to provide additional facts as re quested in the August 10 Order, and because the August 11 and 14 letters do not cure the procedural deficiencies identified in the August 10 Order, the court must deny the pending portions of the Rule 48(a) Motion. 8
...
8 The court reiterates that due to the procedural deficiencies in McCotter's submissions, the court in this Order does not reach Rule 48(a)'s substantive component: here, whether the Department has provided a "substantial" reason for the proposed dismissal of Counts One and Five. 9 Here, the court clarifies that the number of reasons the government may proffer for its dismissal decision is of zero relevence. Courts can and do routinely grant Rule 48(a) motions supported by just one proffered ra tionale-so long as that reason is accompanied by sufficient factual information. Such was the case in, for example, Associate Judge Todd E. Edelman's recent decision to grant the government's Rule 48(a) motion in United States v. Heam, 2026 CF2 010237 (TEE) (D.C. Super. Ct. Aug. 6,
...
In sum, Rule 48(a) requires the government to submit both rea sons for the requested dismissal and sufficient factual support for those reasons. (Id. at 20.) For the reasons thoroughly explained in the August 10 Order, and the additional reasons above, McCotter's unsubstantiated, conclusory statements may amount to reasons for his requested dismissal, but they do not also serve as sufficient underlying facts in support of those reasons. As a result, Rule 48(a)'s procedural requirements are not met, and the court must deny the Department's Motion to dismiss Counts One and Five. 11
